https://www.telegraph.co.uk/art/artists/.subtitle: Climate activists attacked Old Masters and Damien Hirst went up in smoke as the art world was turned on it head
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/art/artists/.text:
Perhaps it seems strange to ­begin a review of the past year during the dog days of 1566. But bear with me, because I ­believe that the fit of destructive energy that erupted in north-west Europe four-and-a-half centuries ago, as ­rioting Calvinists wrecked churches and convents across the Low Countries, may help to clarify the turbulence that has beset the art world in 2022.The Dutch called that spate of iconoclastic fury the Beeldenstorm (image storm). Over time, the term came to refer to any outbreak of iconoclasm during the Reformation. And if the past year in art has been characterised by anything, it’s the thunderclouds of iconoclasm once again gathering overhead – though, this time, the Beeldenstorm is l­ashing not only Europe but also the wider world.The warning signs of more ­trouble ahead – after the tempest of two years ago, when Edward Colston’s statue was toppled in ­Bristol – were already apparent at the start of the year, when a man scaled the facade of Broadcasting House and ­hammered at Eric Gill’s statue of Prospero and Ariel while shouting “paedophile”. The following day, news broke that a Russian security guard in a cultural centre in Ekaterinburg had scribbled crude eyes upon faceless figures in an avant-garde Soviet painting.The latter attack was so absurd, it was almost comical – and, for a while, it was possible to think that the iconoclasts were lone wolves. A troubled American tourist, furious that his demand for an impromptu audience with Pope Francis had been denied, damaged a couple of ancient busts at the Vatican. Even Damien Hirst, in a desperate midlife bid for publicity, incinerated ­thousands of his own paintings. For anyone who believes in ­auguries, the new spirit of topsy-turvydom was confirmed by an announcement that a late, unfinished abstract by the Dutch modernist Piet Mondrian (whose birth, 150 years ago, was ­celebrated in The Hague) has, for the past 75 years on display in a ­German museum, been hanging upside down.Yet the trouble with iconoclasm, as that 16th-century Beeldenstorm reminds us, is that it’s catching, like the plague. Above all, 2022 will be remembered for climate activists broadening their protests from motorways to museums. Over the past year, as if following an atrocious recipe from The Activist Cookbook, copycat campaigners (or vandals; delete as appropriate) have hurled tomato soup over Vincent van Gogh’s Sunflowers in the National Gallery; lobbed mashed potato at a view of haystacks by Claude Monet in a German museum; and, in the most bizarre case, perpetrated by a man posing as an old lady in a wheelchair visiting the Louvre, smeared a cream cake across the glass that ­protects the Mona Lisa.
That’s a full three-course meal of protest – although the activists didn’t restrict themselves to com­estibles. To make their point (calling for an end to fossil fuel), they also, variously, glued themselves to Sandro Botticelli’s Primavera at the Uffizi, scrawled blue ink across a set of Andy Warhol screenprints at the National Gallery of ­Australia and, last month, poured a viscous black concoction, smuggled into Vienna’s Leopold Museum inside a hot-water bottle, over a painting by Gustav Klimt.One remarkable aspect of this vexing phenomenon has been the humming-and-hawing of museums around the world in response. A century or so ago, when the suffragettes staged considerably more ­violent and shocking protests inside our galleries, the authorities were furious. Certainly, there was little sympathy for the “desperados” behind the attacks – although now, of course, suffrage is something that, in Britain, we hold dear.Today, museums prefer to tread a finer line, hoping to deter the ­protests (despite the activists’ claim that only artworks displayed behind ­protective glass are ­targeted), while simultaneously ­recognising the ­justness of their cause. A recent statement by the International Council of Museums (ICOM) described museums as “allies” of the activists “in facing the common threat of climate change”.Even a generation ago, such a confused response would have been unthinkable – yet today’s Beeldenstorm doesn’t only take the form of physical attacks. The most lasting effect of the current flare-up of iconoclastic fervour may be the destruction of old certainties about what museums and galleries are even for.
This year, for instance, the director of an Italian contemporary-art museum suggested to me that ­fundamental art-historical concepts, defined during the Enlightenment, were now imperilled, after decades during which postcolonial studies have dominated academia. “There are pressures on the existence and survival of this Western thing called art,” she said blithely, before adding: “And I really don’t care if it exists or not.”Such a radical shift in professional opinion was reflected in another ICOM statement, offering a controversial (and wordy) new definition of a museum. The director of an important cultural institution in Germany, whom I met recently, précised it as follows: that a museum is no longer primarily “a place for objects” (ie, somewhere culturally significant where artefacts are preserved), but “first a place for people and communities and their interests”. Arguably, the British Museum’s brilliant Stonehenge exhibition exemplified this new approach, by being less interested in the trilithons and sar­sens than the ancient “communities” who gathered at them.“Objects versus people” may sound like an arcane debate, but isn’t: rather, ICOM’s definition has upended decades of orthodoxy regarding what museums are for, and how they’re run – and corro­borates the new, ethically minded puritanism that’s abroad. One ­ongoing conundrum is the inter­national debate over restitution – whether Western museums are morally obliged to return objects looted during the age of imperialism (something the British Museum still resists, although it’s fast ­becoming a lone voice).
Moreover, to combat any impression that they’re complicit with the villainy of empire, many museums now give prominence to indigenous perspectives. Arguably, this reflects a wider transfer in power from the West to the global South. It’s ­striking that the top spot in the new edition of ArtReview’s Power 100 list of the art world’s movers and shakers went to the Indonesian artist collective Ruangrupa, who this year, amid much controversy, curated ­Documenta, the quinquennial ­exhibition of contemporary art held in ­Germany. And, early next year, the National Gallery will ­present an exhibition of work by the Indian a­rtist Nalini Malani, who explicitly says that “classical Western paintings… are not sacrosanct” and “have to be looked at in a different way”. An iconoclast’s target, of course, is never sacred.Pity the poor curator wheeled out to justify Malani’s critique of, as he puts it in the press release, “Western male hegemony”. Although, looking back at the year’s finest exhibitions – the National Gallery’s grand survey of Raphael’s career; a stunner at the Courtauld that gathered (against all odds) 16 of Van Gogh’s self-portraits; Tate Modern’s Cézanne – perhaps he has a point: why didn’t the stand-out shows shine a light on female ­artists? (Aside from Gagosian Gallery’s well-connected Friends and Relations, remarkable for the ­quality of its privately held loans, a glut of shows about Lucian Freud, mostly marking the 100th anniversary of his birth, certainly started to feel like overkill.)Yet, several did; I was taken, for instance, by Tate’s immaculate celebration of the Polish artist ­Magdalena Abakanowicz. Has there been a more propitious time to be a woman making, curating or writing about art? Almost every living artist I’m most excited about happens to be female: Marguerite Humeau, Anne Imhof, Rachel Jones, Allison Katz, Tala Madani, Joanna Piotrowska, Christina Quarles, Andra Ursuta.
In a sign of just how far the pendulum has swung from “Western male hegemony”, about 90 per cent of the artists selected by curator Cecilia Alemani for The Milk of Dreams, her much-lauded exhibition for the 59th Venice Biennale, were women, too. (Touchingly, they included Paula Rego, who died in June.) Alemani’s show, incidentally, also confirmed another recent ­tendency: that surrealism is once again a viable, vital approach within contemporary art.For black female artists, now more feted than ever, 2022 turned into a march of triumph. Following Frank Auerbach, Henry Moore, and Bridget Riley, Britain’s Sonia Boyce won the Golden Lion (for best pavilion) at Venice, where America’s Simone Leigh was also honoured. Veronica Ryan won the Turner Prize and Ingrid Pollard was shortlisted, while, in a move the likes of which I cannot recall, Tate Britain restaged Lynette Yiadom-Boakye’s mid-career survey, after it was cut short, two years ago, by lockdown.In March, east London’s Chisenhale Gallery unveiled a spectacular new body of vivid, seemingly luminescent semi-abstract paintings by Rachel Jones. In October, Hauser & Wirth opened an exhibition, to rave reviews, by the African-American figurative painter Amy Sherald. Of course, many male artists made headlines: Jeff Koons, who wants to send sculptures to the moon; Michael Heizer, whose monumental land-art sculpture City was finally unveiled in the Nevada desert; and, unexpectedly, Brad Pitt, who debuted nine sculptures in a Finnish museum. Yet, at least within the art world, 2022 may go down as the year when cracks in the patri­archy finally became irreparable.
